A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability).

Provenance, kept so that a TRACE Research Object (TRO) declaration of the run can be written later from a stored result (metacheck #404; the helpers are in R/provenance.R). Only when code was run (execute = TRUE): * run_results$started_at, run_results$ended_at: when each run of a script started and ended (ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds); NA for a script that was not started. A script run again in a later pass has the times of its last run. A TRO uses them for each trov:TransparentResearchPerformance. * run_results$exit_status: the exit status of the process that ran the script (0 = ended normally); NA when the process did not report one (a time limit, or Docker failing to start the container). * artifacts: one row per file, with stage (deposit: as downloaded from the repository, hashed from the downloaded file; before_run: the run folder just before the first script ran, after metacheck’s own changes, such as rewritten paths and unpacked archives; after_run: only the files the scripts made (status new), changed (changed) or removed (removed), as an unchanged file is the one listed before the run), path (relative to the run folder, as valid UTF-8, a byte of another encoding written as <xx>), size (bytes), sha256, mime_type (by extension, NA when unknown), source (the file’s address in the repository, for deposit). The package libraries metacheck installs in the run folder are left out, as are metacheck’s own files there (a script’s runner, and the statistical output it writes in statistical_output/). Files metacheck itself copied or made between passes (see modifications, output_copied, file_placed) show in after_run too. A TRO uses the rows as trov:ResearchArtifacts and each stage as a trov:ArtifactArrangement. * modifications$sha256_before, modifications$sha256_after: the hash of the changed script as downloaded and as it ran; NA when the script is not at the same path in both (a script made from an R Markdown file). * environment: the system that ran the code (trov:TransparentResearchSystem in a TRO): metacheck_version, started_at, ended_at, host (R version, platform, operating system), sandbox, network_isolated (TRUE only when every Docker run had --network none; the process sandbox does not stop the network), internet, timeout_per_script, total_timeout, python_local (the Python run outside Docker and its version), and docker: runs (for each kind of run, r_run, r_install, python_run, python_install, the image and the docker run arguments, such as --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, the process limit and the memory and processor limits) and images (for each image, its ID and digests from docker image inspect, its creation time and the R and Python versions its environment declares).

run_results$checked says what the run of each script shows about the code, in five groups, so that a script that does not reproduce is kept apart from one the check could not test: ran (it ran to the end); code_error (it did not reproduce: it stopped with an error of the code or the deposit, could not be read, or needs a file the deposit does not hold); dependency (a package or program was not available: a package that could not be installed or was not loaded, a program outside R and Python, a system library, or R crashing in a package’s compiled code); time (it did not finish within the time limit for one script, or was not started because the time for all scripts had run out); and not_checkable (it could not be checked automatically: it needs a person, the internet, a key or another setting of the authors’ computer, one platform such as Google Colab, Windows or OpenSAFELY, more memory than the run allows, a file that was not downloaded, a screen, or a program that runs it, or it is a file of a package of the code that Python runs only as a module of that package). It is NA for files run inside another script, files that are not an analysis, files not read, and a Docker failure. summary_table counts each group (repro_ran_n, repro_code_error_n, repro_dependency_n, repro_time_n, repro_not_checkable_n), and the report’s first sentence gives them. The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Raw milk consumption is a controllable source of foodborne pathogen exposure in the United States (US), yet existing national estimates of raw milk consumption behaviors are outdated and do not capture emerging factors such as consumers' trusted information sources, sociopolitical influences, and at-home risk mitigation behaviors. We conducted a nationally representative cross-sectional survey of n=1078 US adults to estimate the prevalence of raw milk consumption and at-home thermal treatment practices and identify predictors of these behaviors. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to evaluate predictors of raw milk consumption and thermal treatment behavior using adjusted odds ratios (aORs). Among 1,075 eligible respondents, 15% consumed raw milk in the last six months, including 5% exclusively and 10% in addition to pasteurized milk. In multivariable analysis, raw milk consumption was independently associated with younger age, cohabitation with high-risk individuals for foodborne infections (including children ≤5 years of age, and elderly, pregnant or immunocompromised individuals) who had consumed raw milk, and perceptions of raw milk taste and safety. Adults aged ≥55 years had lower odds of consumption than those aged 18-24 years (aOR, 0.05; 95% CI, 0.02-0.15), while those living with a high-risk household member who consumed raw milk had higher odds of consumption (aOR, 4.39; 95% CI, 2.69-7.22). Perceiving raw milk to have higher risk of causing illness was associated with lower odds of raw milk consumption (aOR: 0.32, 95% CI: 0.17-0.62) compared to believing the risk to be equal across milk types, and thermal treatment was reported by 38% of exclusive raw milk consumers (n=58) and 47% of consumers of both milk types (n=106). Raw milk consumption in the US appears to be substantially more common than previously reported and shaped by factors such as taste, safety, and household raw milk consumption among high-risk individuals for foodborne infections. The proportion of raw milk consumers already practicing at-home thermal treatment suggests a potential opportunity for risk mitigation.

Key Words:

Unpasteurized milk, consumer behavior, risk perception, food safety, heating

Introduction

Raw milk, or milk that has not undergone pasteurization, is a known vehicle of foodborne exposure with pathogens such as Salmonella spp., pathogenic Escherichia coli, Campylobacter spp., Staphylococcus aureus, Brucella spp., Coxiella burnetii, and Listeria monocytogenes 1 . In the United States (US), human consumption of raw dairy products is associated with 840 times more illnesses and 45 times more hospitalizations compared to consumption of pasteurized dairy products when adjusted for servings consumed 2 . Multiple outbreak investigations have linked raw milk consumption to hospitalization and death, including 75 outbreaks with 675 illnesses during 2013-2018 alone 1, 3, 4 . In the US, raw milk access varies by state, with regulations ranging from prohibitions on sale to allowances for retail or on-farm sales, cow-or herd-share programs, and sales labeled for animal consumption 5.

Despite these risks, a 2016 nationally representative survey estimated that ~4-5% of US adults consume raw milk annually 6 . Consumers are primarily younger adults, rural residents, and individuals in states with legal sale access 6, 7 . Concerningly, a substantial proportion of consumers report living with individuals at high risk for foodborne infections, including children and older adults 6, 7 . Beyond demographic patterns, raw milk consumption is shaped by beliefs about perceived health and safety benefits, many of which are not supported by scientific evidence. Proponents of raw milk consumption claim that it is more nutritious than pasteurized milk and may reduce lactose intolerance, allergies, and asthma 8 . Prior studies demonstrate that perceived benefits often undermine established danger in decision-making, with many consumers denying illness risk and expressing low trust in public health authorities 9 . Other motivating factors for raw milk consumption include taste, a desire to support local agriculture, and strong social influences such as family traditions and peer networks 9, 10 . Online platforms have facilitated the dissemination of claims promoting the purported health benefits of raw milk 10 . More broadly, social media has contributed to the rapid spread of nutritional misinformation, potentially influencing consumer food choices and perceptions of risk 11 . Consumer preferences for natural and minimally processed foods may also contribute to the appeal of raw milk 12.

In addition to individual motivations, raw milk consumption is shaped by its legal availability, which varies substantially across the US. The transport of raw milk for human consumption between states is prohibited under federal regulation, as outlined in the Pasteurized Milk Ordinance 13 . However, state-level regulations range from complete prohibition of sales to more permissive guidelines, including the allowance of sales labeled for animal consumption, cow-or herd-share programs, and on-farm or retail sales 5 . These regulations govern commercial access but do not necessarily prohibit consumption; for example, some states permit dairy producers to consume raw milk from their own animals 14.

Regardless of how raw milk is obtained, thermal treatment before consumption represents a potential means of reducing pathogen risk. The most common industrial pasteurization method for fluid milk in the US is high temperature short time (HTST) pasteurization, which involves heating milk to 72°C and holding it for 15 seconds, yielding >5-log reductions of pathogens of concern while preserving its nutritional value 15, 16 . Other common methods include low temperature long time (LTLT), ultrahigh temperature (UHT), and vat pasteurization (Vat-PT) 13.

Historically, when commercially pasteurized milk was less widely available, home boiling was promoted as a practical public health intervention to reduce milk-borne disease. Although guidance for home boiling remains available today, thermal treatment prevalence among contemporary US raw milk consumers remains unknown, despite its investigation as a riskreduction strategy in populations such as Italy and Ethiopia [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] . Understanding this behavior may be particularly important; qualitative research suggests many US raw milk consumers place greater trust in their own food safety practices and familiar producers than in industrial processing methods or government guidance 22.

Despite these insights, critical gaps remain in understanding contemporary raw milk consumption patterns in the US. Previous estimates are now dated and provide limited insight into emerging influences, impacting public health messaging. We sought to address these knowledge gaps through a quantitative, nationally representative survey with the following objectives: to determine the prevalence of raw milk consumption in the US, estimate the frequency of at-home raw milk heating among raw milk consumers, and identify predictors of these behaviors.

Methods

Study Population and Questionnaire Survey Administration.

The questionnaire survey was developed to evaluate consumer perceptions and behaviors regarding raw and pasteurized milk.

The target population consisted of adults (i.e., aged ≥18 years) residing in the US. The survey was administered by Qualtrics Research Services (QRS) 23 from February 14-17, 2025, with a target sample size of 1,000 participants. QRS used demographic quotas for sex, age, geographic region, and education level to approximate the US adult population. The full questionnaire is provided in Supplementary Table S1, and additional details regarding QRS recruitment and sampling procedures are provided in Supplementary Text S1. Cornell Institutional Review Board (IRB) approved the study protocol as an exemption on January 23, 2025 (protocol number IRB0149147).

Variable Definition and Outcome Modeling.

Table 1 defines the variables used in the statistical analyses and their corresponding survey questions. Whether a respondent had consumed raw milk in the past six months (Q1) and at-home thermal treatment behavior among raw milk consumers (Q2; presented only to respondents who in Q1 responded "Raw dairy milk" or "Both raw and pasteurized dairy milk") were defined as the primary and secondary outcomes of interest, respectively. Perceptions of taste (Q5), nutrition beliefs (Q6), illness risk (Q7), cohabitation with high-risk individuals for foodborne illness who have consumed raw milk in the past six months (Q4), and H5N1-related milk safety concern (Q8), as well as trusted information source (Q3), were defined as predictors of interest. The H5N1 milk safety question was included to capture how the newly emerged influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b avian influenza (bird flu) outbreak in dairy cattle, ongoing during survey administration, may have affected respondents' raw milk perceptions and behaviors. Age (Q9), sex at birth (Q10), geographic region (Q11), education level (Q12), and political orientation (Q13) were assessed as potential confounders (Table 1).

The primary outcome (raw milk consumption; Q1) was dichotomized into two versions to differentiate between distinct consumption patterns: Model R Any for any raw milk consumption (including those who consumed raw milk exclusively or in addition to pasteurized milk) and Model R Exclusive for exclusive raw milk consumption in the last 6 months (Table 1) and identify their predictors.

The secondary outcome, at-home thermal treatment of raw milk, was assessed by asking how frequently respondents heated raw milk (e.g., by boiling or steaming) prior to consumption (Q2).

Responses were dichotomized based on consistency of heating: respondents reporting heating more than half the time or always were categorized as consistent heaters, and those reporting heating half the time or less (never, less than half the time, or approximately half the time) served as the reference group. This threshold was selected because infrequent heating still results in regular consumption of unheated raw milk. Respondents who selected "Prefer not to answer" were coded as missing. Because this question applied only to raw milk consumers, the analysis was restricted to respondents reporting raw milk consumption in the past six months and was conducted separately among all raw milk consumers (Model T Any ; including those who consumed raw milk exclusively or in addition to pasteurized milk) and among exclusive raw milk consumers (Model T Exclusive ).

Predictor Variables Preparation and Recoding.

For perceived taste (Q5), nutrition beliefs (Q6), perceived illness risk (Q7), and H5N1 safety concern (Q8), responses of "I don't know," and "Prefer not to answer" were combined into a single "Uncertain/No response" category, as these responses accounted for a large proportion of the sample for these questions, particularly Q5 and Q6. For Q5, Q6, and Q7, "They are equal" was retained as a distinct response category, as it represented a substantive belief about each question rather than uncertainty, while "I don't know" and "Prefer not to answer" were grouped together, representing a lack of any strong opinion. For trusted information source (Q3), respondents who selected "prefer not to answer" or were also categorized as "Uncertain/No response" category as well.

Cohabitation with pre-defined high-risk individuals for foodborne illness within the household who consumed raw milk in the last 6 months (Q4) was assessed with a multiple-select question.

For analysis, responses were used to ascertain counts of each high-risk subgroup for descriptive purposes. Additionally, a binary indicator for cohabitation with a high-risk individual who consumed raw milk was created to identify respondents whose household included at least one high-risk individual (i.e., children aged 5 or younger, adults aged 65 or older, immunocompromised individuals, or pregnant individuals) who had consumed raw milk in the past six months, compared to those who indicated that this did not apply to any member of their household (Table 1). Respondents who declined to answer this question (n=24) were grouped with those reporting no cohabitation with a high-risk individual who consumed raw milk for multivariable analysis. Age (Q9) was collapsed from six categories into five, with respondents aged 55-64 and 65 or over combined into a single "55 or older" group. Sex at birth (Q10) was analyzed as reported; respondents who selected any option aside from male or female or declined to answer (n = 3) were coded as missing and excluded from models including this variable. Geographic region (Q11) was derived from self-reported state of residence and categorized according to U.S.

Census Bureau regions 24 (Table 1). Education level (Q12) was collapsed into four categories: "high school or less" (below high school, some high school, high school graduate or GED; reference category); "some college or technical" (technical/trade/vocational school, some college or two-year associate degree); "college graduate" (four-year degree); and "graduate or professional" (post-graduate or professional training). Political orientation (Q13) was collapsed into three categories: respondents identifying as strong Democrat, not very strong Democrat, or independent leaning Democrat were classified as "Democrat"; those identifying as strong Republican, not very strong Republican, or independent leaning Republican were classified as "Republican"; and those identifying as independent leaning toward neither party or reporting another party affiliation were classified as "Independent/Other." Respondents who declined to answer the education or political orientation questions were coded as missing and excluded from models including this variable.

Statistical Analysis.

All statistical analyses were performed using R. To verify the national representativeness of the sample, we compared the demographic characteristics of the survey participants with the 2020 US Census data 25 using a one-sample z test. Variables included in these comparisons were geographic region, age, sex, and education level.

In statistical analyses of associations for two versions of the primary outcome (Models R Any and R Exclusive ), we first performed univariable logistic regression between each predictor and each of the outcomes of interest. Odds ratios (ORs) and the associated Wald 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated as measures of association. To ensure potential confounders were not excluded prematurely, all variables with a p-value < 0.10 were carried over into multivariable analysis.

For the two versions of the secondary outcome (Models T Any and T Exclusive ), associations between candidate predictors and thermal treatment were first assessed using the original five-level heating frequency response, prior to dichotomization. Fisher's exact tests were used in place of chi-square tests due to small expected cell counts. Predictors were then examined using the dichotomized outcome following the same screening and model selection procedure described above (i.e., heating always or more than half the time vs approximately half the time or less frequently/never), and analyses were repeated under two alternative dichotomization thresholds (heating at least half the time vs less than half the time or never; any frequency of heating versus never) to assess whether findings depended on a particular categorization. Similarly to the univariable analysis of the primary outcome, all variables with a p-value < 0.10 were carried over into multivariable analysis, and corresponding multivariable models were constructed.

Multivariable Model Selection and Validation.

Final model selection for an outcome of interest was performed using forward stepwise selection based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). For each final model, two-way interactions between significant predictors were evaluated after variable selection, followed by the Benjamini-Hochberg corrections for multiple comparisons of the interaction terms. An adjusted Odds Ratio (aOR) was used as a measure of the association between a specific predictor and an outcome, while controlling for other variables in the final model. Model performance for the primary outcomes was assessed using the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test and the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

Results

Study Population.

The final number of responses was 1,078, as QRS received more responses than anticipated before closing the survey. The responses were determined to be nationally representative relative to the 2020 US Census with respect to geographic region (p=0.91), sex (p=0.99), age (p=0.23), and level of education (p=0.43) using one-sample z tests. After excluding respondents who did not meet eligibility criteria (i.e., under 18 (n = 3) or not US residents (n = 0)), there were 1,075 remaining eligible responses (Table 2). Those who either declined to answer the question regarding milk consumption or indicated that they did not consume any dairy milk (n = 177) were removed. This yielded a final analytical sample of 898 respondents evaluated in the univariable and multivariable statistical analysis.

Descriptive Statistics.

Of the eligible respondents (n=1,075), most reported consuming only pasteurized milk (68%) in the past six months, while 15% reported not consuming dairy milk at all and were therefore excluded from further analysis. In this sample, 10% of respondents consumed raw milk alongside pasteurized milk, while 5% consumed only raw milk (Table 2).

Thermal treatment of raw milk (e.g., by microwave, boiling, or steaming) was practiced to some extent by a large portion of raw milk consumers, with 87% of raw and pasteurized milk drinkers reporting heating "Less than half the time" or more, and 71% of exclusive raw milk consumers doing so (Table 3). Those who consumed a combination of raw and pasteurized milk were more likely to practice at-home heating of raw milk overall, with responses concentrated in the intermediate frequency categories (47% reported heating "More than half the time" or "Always"). Exclusive consumers were more likely to report never heating their raw milk (29% vs. 13% of non-exclusive consumers), while both exclusive and non-exclusive consumers selected "Always" at a very similar frequency of about one-quarter.

Raw Milk (Models R) Univariable analysis.

Predictors of Any Raw Milk Consumption (Model R Any ). Univariable logistic regression on

the analytical sample of 898 participants revealed several statistically significant demographic and perception-related associations with any raw milk consumption (either raw only or both pasteurized and raw) (Table 4). Males showed slightly higher odds of consumption than females (OR: 1.58, 95% CI: 1.12-2.24). Geographically, residents in the Northeast and South were each almost twice as likely to have consumed both raw and pasteurized milk compared to those in the Midwest (p < 0.05 for both).

Compared with respondents who viewed raw and pasteurized milk as nutritionally "Equal", those who selected "Pasteurized better" (OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.20-0.53) or "Raw better" (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.38-0.95) had lower odds of consuming both raw and pasteurized milk. For taste, respondents who indicated "Pasteurized better" had significantly lower odds of consuming both raw and pasteurized milk (OR 0.19, 95% CI 0.12-0.32), as did those who were grouped as "Uncertain/No response" (OR: 0.03, CI: 0.02-0.06) (Table 4). Regarding perception of H5N1 risk, respondents concerned about both, selecting "Yes, if consuming either raw or pasteurized milk" (OR: 2.79, 95% CI: 1.54-5.22) or "Yes, if consuming pasteurized milk" (OR: 2.69, 95% CI: 1.19-6.01) had significantly higher odds of consuming both raw and pasteurized milk compared to those indicating "No" concern, while concern specific to raw milk ("Yes, if consuming raw milk") was not significantly associated with consumption (p = 0.930). Perceived illness risk was also influential; compared to believing "They are equal", all other selections ("Pasteurized higher [risk]", "Raw milk higher [risk]", or "Uncertain/no response") showed significantly lower odds of consumption. Trusted information source was a significant predictor of consumption as well. Compared to those indicating the most trust in "Doctors or nurses", those listening to "Social media influencers", "Friends or family", and "Farmers" all showed significantly higher odds of consumption, while "Government officials" and "Professors or researchers" were not significantly associated with consumption (Table 4). Cohabitation with high-risk individuals who had consumed raw milk in the past six months was one of the strongest predictors in the univariable analysis; participants answering "Yes" to living with at-risk members who consumed raw milk had significantly higher odds of consumption themselves (OR: 7.62, 95% CI: 5.23-11.17, p < 0.001).

Predictors of Exclusive Raw Milk Consumption (Model R Exclusive ).

In univariable logistic regression to identify predictors associated with exclusive raw milk consumption (Table 5), many predictors aligned with the results for Model R Any , with a few important differences. Age remained a significant predictor for exclusive consumption (p < 0.001), but the protective effect of the older age group was slightly less pronounced than in Model R Any . Respondents over the age of 55 were still the least likely group to consume raw milk exclusively (OR: 0.05, 95% CI: 0.01-0.13) compared to the 18-24 reference group. While sex and geographic region were significant predictors of raw milk consumption in Model R Any , they did not show a statistically significant association with exclusive raw milk consumption.

Cohabitation with a high-risk individual who had consumed raw milk remained a strong predictor of exclusive raw milk consumption; those cohabiting with such an individual had significantly higher odds of exclusive consumption compared to those who did not (OR: 8.62, 95% CI: 4.96-15.32). Taste perception remained a significant motivating factor, with those believing raw milk tasted better having significantly higher odds of exclusive consumption compared to those perceiving the taste as equal (OR: 2.93, 95% CI: 1.45-6.26), while those in the "Uncertain/no response" taste preference category had significantly lower odds (OR: 0.14, 95% CI: 0.05-0.36). For nutrition beliefs, only the "Uncertain/No response" category differed significantly from the reference (OR: 0.23, 95% CI: 0.09-0.55). Perceived illness risk was significant only for those believing raw milk posed greater risk, with that group having lower odds of exclusive consumption (OR: 0.39, 95% CI: 0.19-0.86), and unlike in Model R Any , H5N1 safety concern was not a significant predictor of exclusive consumption at any level. Trusted information source continued to be an influential predictor in this univariable analysis. Friends and family and social media influencers remained significant predictors compared to medical professionals, with higher odds of consumption, while farmers, which were significant in Model R Any , were not significant predictors of exclusive consumption.

Multivariable Analysis

Multivariable logistic regression models were constructed for both Model R Any and Model R Exclusive of the main outcome (raw milk consumption) to identify independent predictors of behavior.

Model R Any : Any Raw Milk Consumption.

The final multivariable model for Model R Any demonstrated adequate calibration and fit, as validated by the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-offit test (χ2 = 3.137 df = 8, p = 0.926), and excellent predictive discrimination, AUC-ROC of 0.912. In this multivariable Model R Any (Figure 1), several factors remained significant predictors after controlling for other variables. Cohabitation with high-risk individuals who have consumed raw milk was a strong independent predictor; respondents who reported cohabitation with a high-risk individual who consumed raw milk had 4.39 times higher odds of consuming raw milk themselves compared to those who did not (95% CI: 2.69-7.22). Perceptions of taste were also strong predictors of any raw milk consumption. With taste being equal as the reference category, respondents who believed pasteurized milk tasted better had significantly lower odds of consumption (aOR: 0.22, 95% CI: 0.11-0.40), as did those with Uncertain/No response taste preferences (aOR: 0.04, 95% CI: 0.02-0.10). Believing that raw milk tasted better was not significantly associated with consumption.

Safety concerns regarding H5N1 were also influential. Using "No" as the reference, respondents who answered "Yes, if consuming either raw or pasteurized milk" had the highest odds of any raw milk consumption (aOR: 6.60, 95% CI: 2.90-15.62), followed by those in the "Uncertain/No response" group (aOR: 2.67, 95% CI: 1.17-6.27). Perceived illness risk showed significant prediction influence as well; respondents who believed raw milk posed a greater illness risk had lower odds of any raw milk consumption compared to those who believed the risk was equal between milk types (aOR: 0.32, 95% CI: 0.17-0.62). Age remained inversely associated with consumption, with the 55 or older age group showing the lowest odds compared to the 18-24 reference group (aOR: 0.05, 95% CI: 0.02-0.15).

The tests of two-way interactions in this final model identified a significant interaction between taste and cohabitation with high-risk individuals who consumed raw milk in likelihood ratio testing (χ² = 9.38, df = 3, p = 0.026). However, it was one of ten interactions assessed and did not remain significant under the Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing (both adjusted p = 0.256). While the AIC marginally favored the model including the interaction, given the added complexity of the model, the limited size of the compared groups, difficulties in the interpretation of the "Uncertain/No response" category in this model and the fact that this interaction was not confirmed in Model R Exclusive , the interaction was not retained in the final model R Any and is reported as an exploratory finding in supplementary materials (Supplementary Text S2 and Figure S1).

Model R Exclusive : Exclusive Raw Milk Consumption.

The final multivariable model for exclusive raw milk showed a similar pattern of predictors. Cohabitation with a high-risk individual who consumed raw milk remained the dominant predictor, with those respondents having 7.41 times higher odds of being exclusive raw milk consumers compared to those not cohabitating with a high-risk individual who consumed raw milk (95% CI: 3.81-15.06). Taste perception was also strongly associated. Using "Equal" as the reference, respondents who believed raw milk tasted better had significantly higher odds of exclusive consumption (aOR: 4.47, 95% CI: 2.02-10.49). Age remained inversely associated with exclusive consumption, with the 55+ group showing the lowest odds compared to the 18-24 reference group (aOR: 0.11, 95% CI: 0.03-0.37). H5N1 safety concern and perceived illness risk were evaluated as candidate predictors but were not retained in the final model, as their inclusion did not improve model fit.

We evaluated the model for 2-way interactions but identified none. This model displayed good discrimination, with an AUC of 0.879, and the Hosmer-Lemeshow test supported that it was an adequate fit (p = 0.723).

Thermal Treatment (Models T).

Univariable and Multivariable Analysis. We examined the secondary outcome, at-home thermal treatment, among participants who reported consuming raw milk in the past six months. Thermal treatment was assessed by asking how frequently respondents heated raw milk (e.g., by boiling or steaming) prior to consumption (Q2). Heating frequency differed significantly between those who consume both raw and pasteurized milk and exclusive raw milk consumers (Fisher's exact p = 0.03), driven primarily by the proportion reporting no thermal treatment: 29% (n = 17) of exclusive raw milk consumers reported never heating their milk, compared to 13% (n = 14) of those consuming both raw and pasteurized milk. Additionally, among participants who consumed both raw and pasteurized milk (n = 106), 47% (n = 50) reported heating raw milk more than half the time or always, compared to 38% (n = 22) of those consuming exclusively raw milk (n = 58).

Associations between candidate predictors and thermal treatment were first assessed using the original five-level heating frequency response, before any dichotomization. Among all raw milk consumers (Model T Any; (n=164), comprised of those who consume both raw and pasteurized milk (n=106) and those who drink raw milk exclusively (n=58), with the description of each model being more comprehensively described in supplementary table S2), education level showed the strongest association (p = 0.008) followed by taste (p = 0.013); nutritional beliefs did not reach significance at the 5% threshold. Among exclusive raw milk consumers (Model T Exclusive ; n=58), perceived illness risk was the only predictor associated with heating frequency (p = 0.016). The analysis was then repeated using a dichotomized outcome, with respondents reporting heating "more than half the time" or "always" classified as practicing consistent thermal treatment and all others serving as the reference group. This threshold was selected because infrequent heating still results in regular consumption of unheated raw milk. Among all raw milk consumers (Model T Any ), education level and nutrition beliefs were the only predictors that met the univariable screening threshold (p <0.10) and were carried forward to multivariable analysis. Subsequently, they were retained in the final multivariable model. Compared to respondents with a high school education or less, those with graduate or professional training had substantially higher odds of consistent thermal treatment (aOR: 13.87, 95% CI: 3.86-68.83), while differences for college graduates and those with some college or technical training were not significant. The proportion of respondents reporting consistent thermal treatment increased with education, from 32% among those with a high school education or less to 83% among those with graduate or professional training, and no respondent in the highest education group reported never heating raw milk. Respondents who were uncertain about the relative nutritional value of raw and pasteurized milk had lower odds of consistent thermal treatment compared to those who believed the two were nutritionally equivalent (aOR: 0.07, 95% CI: 0.01-0.36), although this estimate was based on a small group in which only 2 of 17 respondents reported consistent thermal treatment. Beliefs that either milk type was nutritionally superior were not significantly associated with heating behavior. This model demonstrated acceptable discrimination (AUC = 0.724) and adequate calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow χ² = 1.90, df = 3, p = 0.594). It should be noted that the education association was driven largely by a small group of graduate-educated respondents (n = 23), and the nutrition beliefs association reflected lower odds of heating among respondents who expressed uncertainty (n = 17) rather than any belief. These findings should therefore be interpreted with caution. Among exclusive raw milk consumers (Model T Exclusive , n = 55), only political orientation met the screening threshold (p<0.1), and Republican orientation was not significantly associated with thermal treatment compared to Democrat orientation (aOR: 2.91, 95% CI: 0.88-10.28). This model showed weaker discrimination (AUC = 0.627); the Hosmer-Lemeshow test was not applicable, as a model containing a single categorical predictor yields fewer distinct fitted probabilities than the number of groups required for the test.

The dichotomized univariable analysis was repeated under two alternative definitions: (i) heating at least half the time versus less than half, and (ii) any heating versus never. The association with nutrition beliefs was stable in direction and magnitude across all three definitions (uncertain vs. nutritionally equivalent: aOR 0.07-0.11, all p ≤ 0.005). The association between education and thermal treatment was consistent in direction across definitions; under both alternative definitions, all respondents with graduate or professional training were classified as thermally treating their raw milk, so an odds ratio could not be estimated for that group. The association with political orientation among exclusive consumers was inconsistent in direction and magnitude across definitions (aOR: 2.91, 1.44, and 0.56) and did not reach significance under any.

Discussion

This nationally representative survey was designed to determine the prevalence of raw milk consumption in the US, the proportion of raw milk consumers who heat their milk prior to consumption and identify predictors of these behaviors. The main findings were: (1) raw milk consumption prevalence is higher than previous national estimates, (2) multivariable analyses showed that raw milk consumption was associated with younger age, favorable taste and safety perceptions, and reliance on informal information sources, (3) household vulnerability was one of the strongest predictors of raw milk consumption, and (4) at-home thermal treatment behaviors were fairly common among raw milk consumers.

Higher prevalence of raw milk consumption. Among 1,075 eligible US adult respondents, 15% reported consuming raw milk within the past six months, substantially higher than previous national estimates. Using nationally representative FDA surveys from 2016 and 2019, Lando et al. estimated that 4.4% of US adults had consumed raw milk at least once in the previous 12 months, while only 2% consumed raw milk at least monthly and 1% at least weekly 6 . The authors found no significant differences in raw milk consumption between the 2016 and 2019 surveys. In contrast, our estimate of 15% was observed using a shorter, six-month recall period captured in 2024. A shorter recall period would be expected to capture fewer occasional consumers than a 12-month period, making the substantially higher prevalence observed in our study particularly notable. However, differences in survey design and sampling prevent these estimates from being direct evidence of an increase in raw milk consumption over time. The FDA surveys asked respondents a binary "yes/no" question about whether they had consumed any raw milk in the previous 12 months, explicitly defining raw milk as "milk that was not pasteurized" and noting that it is "often sold off-the-farm or door-to-door" 6 . In contrast, our survey asked respondents to identify which type of dairy milk they had consumed during the previous six months (raw, pasteurized, both, or neither), defined dairy milk as including milk from cows, goats, and sheep, and did not provide additional contextual information about raw milk. Question framing, survey administration, sampling, and the explicit description of raw milk may have influenced responses. Future research using standardized survey methods is needed to confirm the extent of an increase in raw milk consumption and identify contributing factors. The higher prevalence observed in our study may also reflect real changes in consumer behavior such as increased interest in or access to raw milk since previous surveys. Prior research has described increasing consumer interest in local and unprocessed foods and greater availability of unpasteurized dairy products 6 . Legal access may also contribute to consumption; Lando et al.

found that adults living in states where retail sale of raw milk was legal were more likely to report raw milk consumption. In accordance with this, nine of the ten states that amended relevant raw milk laws between 2012 and 2018 expanded legal access, with 27 states permitting raw milk sales by 2019 2, 6 . Given the substantial increase of foodborne disease risk associated with unpasteurized dairy products, even modest increases in raw milk consumption could have important public health implications. Specifically, Costard et al. projected that a doubling of unpasteurized milk and cheese consumption could increase outbreak-related illnesses by approximately 96% 2 . Determining whether our higher prevalence estimate reflects a true increase in consumption is essential for assessing the current and future burden of raw milkassociated foodborne illness.

Respondent age, perceived safety and taste, and reliance on informal information sources

strongly influenced consumption behavior. Our survey found that raw milk consumption is strongly associated with younger age, consistent with prior studies which have similarly identified higher consumption among younger and middle-aged adults 6, 9, 26 . Our results showed perceptions of taste and safety were also among the strongest predictors of raw milk consumption -individuals who believed raw milk tasted equal or better than pasteurized milk, or who perceived similar or lower health risks, had substantially higher odds of raw milk consumption. Previous work has similarly identified sensory characteristics and perceived healthfulness as key motivators of raw milk consumption 22, 26, 27 . Notably, individuals who perceived raw and pasteurized milk as equally risky also had significantly higher odds of raw milk consumption, suggesting that personal perception of the risk (or lack of it) may be a key driver of behavior. Similarly, Markham et al. found that raw milk consumers believed raw milk was safe and disagreed with government warnings 22 . Finally, our finding that taste was one of the strongest predictors of raw milk consumption is consistent with studies reporting that consumers prefer the flavor of raw milk cheeses and perceive products labeled as "raw" to be of higher quality 28 . Together, these findings suggest that consumption is strongly shaped by perceptions of raw milk safety and sensory benefits, calling for more targeted messaging to address these factors. Compared with general food safety instruction, pathogen-specific education has been shown to improve food safety knowledge and reduce high-risk food consumption, including raw milk, particularly among high-risk populations 29 . Communication strategies that focus on general risk warnings may be insufficient to change behavior among consumers who already perceive raw milk as safe or desirable. This point ties directly into respondents' trusted information sources, which were strongly associated with raw milk consumption behavior. Individuals who relied on social media influencers, friends and family, or farmers were significantly more likely to consume raw milk compared to those who relied on medical professionals, highlighting the central role of informal information networks in health-related behaviors. Reliance on informal sources may also make it more difficult for traditional public health messaging, including pathogen-specific food safety education, to reach raw milk consumers. Thus, effective risk communication may require close consideration of the sources and channels through which consumers receive food safety information. Prior work has demonstrated that online and interpersonal sources often shape food safety beliefs more strongly than expert guidance, with consumers relying on these sources when forming perceptions of risk 26 . Online food-related information is often evaluated through rapid, heuristic processes influenced by visual presentation and perceived relevance, rather than careful assessment of evidence or expertise 30 . As a result, narratives that are simplified, emotionally engaging, or personally relevant may disproportionately influence beliefs about food and health.

Specifically, social media can shape nutritional beliefs and diets, with such narratives amplified through these platforms and influencing food choices 11 . Younger individuals may be disproportionately exposed to these forms of content, potentially contributing to observed agerelated differences in consumption patterns 11.

In summary, raw milk consumers are not a homogeneous population but instead differ in their motivations, trusted information sources, and food safety knowledge. This aligns with prior work proposing distinct "mental models" of raw milk consumers, suggesting that understanding these differing perspectives may help inform more effective food safety education and risk communication strategies 31 . Future research should prioritize understanding consumers' motivations for consuming raw milk as a necessary first step toward delivering effective food safety education and risk communication.

Living with high-risk individuals for foodborne infections was one of the strongest predictors of raw milk consumption. Among the 1,075 eligible respondents, 19% reported that at least one household member with high risk for foodborne infection had consumed raw milk in the past six months, including children ≤5 years old, adults ≥65 years old, immunocompromised individuals, or pregnant individuals. Children ≤5 years old (10% of all respondents) and adults ≥65 years old (9%) were the most frequently reported high-risk household members consuming raw milk. Among respondents who consumed raw milk themselves, approximately half reported living with a high-risk household member who also consumed raw milk, compared with 12% of respondents who consumed pasteurized milk only. Consistent with this pattern, living with a high-risk individual who consumed raw milk was one of the strongest and most consistent predictors of respondents' own raw milk consumption across analyses. These findings suggest that raw milk consumption may cluster within households, including households in which individuals at increased risk of severe foodborne illness consume raw milk. This is particularly concerning given that children have been disproportionately represented among reported raw milk-associated illnesses, and both young children and older adults are at increased risk of severe illness following exposure to raw milk pathogens 32 . Recent outbreak underscore these risks, including a 2026 multistate E. coli outbreak linked to raw milk cheese in which more than half of reported cases occurred among children aged five years or younger 33.

As a possible explanation of our findings, households with children or immunocompromised members may be more likely to seek foods they perceive as health-promoting, including raw milk, which is often viewed as more natural, less processed, and beneficial for immunity, allergies, or gut health 34 . This explanation is consistent with studies suggesting that vulnerability may lead people to rely on heuristics rather than more central processing routes of information credibility 35 . For example, parents of children with cancer were more likely to seek out health information but also more likely to believe COVID-19-related misinformation, a pattern attributed to increased stress and greater reliance on heuristic processing 36 . Behavioral frameworks further suggest that heightened perceived concern for health may drive individuals to seek actions that reduce fear, including endorsement of prevention-focused beliefs [35] [36] [37].

However, our survey cannot determine why raw milk consumption clustered within these households; we did not include sufficient follow-up questions to characterize this association, limiting our ability to distinguish motivation from shared household behavior and exposure.

Future work should inquire about presence of an at-risk household member in general, and subsequently their raw milk consumption, as well as assess raw milk consumption directly among high-risk individuals for foodborne infections.

Thermal treatment behaviors were common, although predictors of this behavior were not consistent across analytic approaches. Thermal treatment of raw milk, which may represent an at-home intervention to reduce pathogen risk, was reported more than half the time or always by 47% of respondents consuming both raw and pasteurized milk and 38% of exclusive raw milk consumers. Although the effectiveness of reported thermal treatment practices could not be evaluated, approximately 4 in 10 respondents reported heating raw milk more than half the time or always. This novel finding suggests that US raw milk consumers may be receptive to interventions promoting thermal treatment as a food safety measure, a behavior studied in countries such as Italy and Ethiopia [17] [18] [19] . Additionally, this finding has implications for future food safety risk assessments; existing assessments incorporate consumer behaviors such as storage time and temperature but generally assume that raw milk is consumed without prior household heat treatment 38 . Consequently, failure to account for at-home thermal treatment could bias estimates of pathogen exposure among US raw milk consumers and overestimate the risk of foodborne disease. Future research should assess the effectiveness of at-home thermal treatment of raw milk, including the effects of heating temperature, duration, and storage time before heating.

Education showed a potential association with at-home thermal treatment among all raw milk consumers, although this finding was not consistent across analytic approaches. When heating frequency was examined using the original five-level response, education and perceived taste showed the strongest associations. When thermal treatment was dichotomized, respondents with graduate or professional training had significantly higher odds of consistent thermal treatment than those with a high school education or less. However, this association was driven largely by a small group of graduate-educated respondents (n = 23) and was not observed among exclusive raw milk consumers. Overall, these findings suggest a possible relationship between education and at-home thermal treatment, but larger studies are needed to determine reproducibility and identify other factors related to at-home thermal treatment among raw milk consumers.

Limitations.

While this survey provides novel insight into US raw milk consumption and motivation patterns, there exist certain limitations. Firstly, the prevalence report relies upon the assumption that our sample is representative of the target population. While we confirmed national representativeness by comparing a series of demographic variables with the US census, it is possible that there exist other confounders that would compromise the internal validity of our study. The QRS panel may introduce selection bias toward individuals willing to participate in online surveys, and in general, self-reported data introduces issues of selection and response biases. Further, individuals with stronger opinions about raw milk may have been more likely to complete the survey, introducing self-selection bias that could influence prevalence estimates and observed associations in either direction.

Additionally, while we compared raw milk to pasteurized in survey wording, it is possible that some respondents were unclear of the official definition leading to misclassification. If nondifferential, this misclassification would likely bias results toward the null; however, if differential across respondent groups (e.g., by age or beliefs), the direction of bias is uncertain. It is also possible that respondents who in Q1 reported drinking only pasteurized milk in the past 6 months answered the question comparing raw and pasteurized milk taste (Q5) based on assumptions but may not have ever been in the presence of raw milk. This could introduce response bias and limit interpretation of perceived sensory factors impacting consumption behavior. Furthermore, this survey quantifies at-home heat treatment of raw milk, a previously under-characterized and potentially important risk mitigation measure, but respondents may have interpreted "heating" differently. This misconception could prompt wider confidence intervals due to a smaller sample size and therefore less power, biasing results towards the null, or potentially introducing some nondifferential misclassification. Finally, there could have been residual confounding from unmeasured variables (e.g., cultural or dietary patterns) that may have influenced variable associations through missing data.

Conclusion

Our study reports that raw milk consumption frequency among US adults has considerably increased in recent years. Why cannot be definitively stated; our findings suggest that engaging in raw milk consumption is influenced by an interplay of sensory perception, household context, and risk interpretation, rather than a single dominant factor. Further, the quantification of consumers heating their milk at home represents a previously under-characterized and important risk mitigation measure. Thermal treatment behaviors were not found to be an extension of consumption patterns but were rather shaped by distinct belief systems and sociopolitical factors. Our insights will be valuable in informing policymakers about the extent and potential modifiers of US raw milk consumption. Categorical: Belief about how the taste of raw milk compares to pasteurized milk. Response options: "Raw is better," "Pasteurized is better," "They are equal" (reference category), with "I don't know" and "Prefer not to answer" grouped as "Uncertain/No response".

Q5 Predictor Nutrition Beliefs

Categorical: Belief about the nutritional value of raw vs. pasteurized milk. Response options: "Raw is better," "Pasteurized is better," "They are equal" (reference category), with "I don't know" and "Prefer not to answer" grouped as "Uncertain/No response".

Q6

Predictor Perceived Illness Risk Categorical: Belief about which type of milk is more likely to cause illness. Response options: "Raw milk," "Pasteurized milk," "They are equal" (reference category), with "I don't know" and "Prefer not to answer" grouped as "Uncertain/No response".

Q7 Predictor H5N1 Milk Safety Concern

Categorical: Belief about whether consumers should worry about milk safety during a bird flu (H5N1) outbreak in dairy cattle. Response options: "Yes, if consuming raw milk," "Yes, if consuming pasteurized milk," "Yes, if consuming either raw or pasteurized milk", and "No" (reference category), with "I don't know", and "Prefer not to answer" grouped as "Uncertain/No response".

Q8

Potential Confounder Age Group Categorical: Self-reported age: 18-24 (reference category), 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, and 55+ (combining 55-64 and 65 or over). Q9

Potential Confounder Sex at Birth Categorical: Sex assigned at birth, Male compared to Female (reference category). Respondents who selected another option or declined to answer were coded as missing and excluded from models including this variable.

Q10

Potential Confounder Geographic Region Categorical: US Census region of current residence, derived from state of residence, categorized as Midwest (reference category), Northeast, South, and West.

Q11 Potential Confounder Education Level

Categorical: Highest level of educational attainment, collapsed into four categories: "High school, equivalent, or less" (reference category), "Some college or technical," "College graduate," and "Graduate or professional." Respondents who declined to answer were coded as missing and excluded from models including this variable.

Q12

Potential Confounder Political Orientation Categorical: Self-described political party orientation, collapsed into three categories: "Democrat" (including Democrat orientation qualified as strong, not very strong, or independent-leaning; reference category), "Republican" (including Republican orientations qualified as strong, not Q13 very strong, or independent-leaning), and "Independent/Other" (identifying as independent leaning toward neither party or reporting another party affiliation). Respondents who declined to answer were coded as missing and excluded from models including this variable.
